lesson.title: Hidden Shifts II: GH→CH & Y→G
lesson.subtitle: The inversion lessons: Nacht↔night, Licht↔light, sagen↔say, gestern↔yesterday

hook.title: The Ghost Letters
hook.content: English words walk around with dead letters: night, light, eight, right, daughter. The gh was once a real sound — a throaty ch, exactly like German's. English spelled it, then stopped saying it. German never stopped: Nacht, Licht, acht, Recht, Tochter. The same inversion runs on the y-side: English softened the ancient g into y (say, day, yesterday), German kept it: sagen, Tag, gestern. You have collected these pairs all trail long — today is the payoff: the complete ghost-letter map, every silent gh in English answered by a sounding ch in German.

footnotes.title: English Did Both Directions
footnotes.content: English vocalized g→y (say, day, way) and silenced gh (night, daughter). German did neither: it kept sagen's g and Nacht's ch. So German is, in both cases, the conservative sibling — the archive where the old sounds still play.

pattern.title: The Complete Ghost Map
pattern.content: gh → ch: night ↔ Nacht, light ↔ Licht, laugh ↔ lachen, daughter ↔ Tochter, eight ↔ acht, right ↔ Recht, might ↔ Macht, knight ↔ Knecht (the word that got noble in English and stayed farmhand in German!), freight ↔ Fracht. y → g: say ↔ sagen, way ↔ Weg, yesterday ↔ gestern, eye ↔ Auge (the g hides mid-word). rain ↔ Regen, nail ↔ Nagel. Double-shift royalty: Tochter carries D→T AND gh→ch; dachte/thought closes the loop you opened in the suppletion lesson. This completes all nine Atlas families — the full decode engine.
pattern.linguist_note: English 'laugh' still spells the gh but pronounces an f — a last derangement. German lachen kept the original [x]. When you say 'ich lache', you are pronouncing what 'I laugh' looked like in 700 AD.

exercises.prompt: The ghost map — match each silent-gh word with its sounding ch twin:
exercises.explanation: English silenced the gh; German still sounds it as ch. The ghost letters were always German ch.

exercises.prompt: Why does English 'say' and German 'sagen' start differently?
options: English vocalized the ancient g into y; German kept the g
exercises.target_answer: English vocalized the ancient g into y; German kept the g
exercises.explanation: Same word, two pronunciations: English wore the g down to y (say, day, way); German kept it audible.
The d hardened to t AND the guttural survived as ch — daughter is the flagship of the double-shift fleet.

exercises.prompt: What English time word is the twin of 'gestern'?
exercises.explanation: yester- and gestern are one word split by the y/g inversion — the same root as say/sagen.

exercises.idea: you're saying goodnight at a friend's place: good night — the light is out
cues: Both ghost-map words sound again in German: Nacht (night) and Licht (light) — gh → ch — then ist aus closes it
exercises.target_answer: Gute Nacht das Licht ist aus
exercises.meaning: Good night! The light is out
exercises.affirmation: You made the silent letters sound — Nacht and Licht built straight from night and light.

vocab_hints.note: aus ↔ out — the T→S twin, here doing 'off' duty

exercises.explanation: Two ghost-map words in one goodnight: Nacht and Licht — gh → ch, both still sounding.

summary.outcome: Read every silent gh as German ch and every English y as German g — all nine Atlas families complete.

use_example.german: Gute Nacht — das Licht ist aus.
use_example.english: Good night — the light is out.

summary.takeaway: gh→ch (Nacht, Licht, acht) and y→g (sagen, gestern): the ghost letters are German sounds English stopped pronouncing.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: Nacht & Licht — the gh→ch inversion: the silent letters of night and light, still sounding in German.

twist.explanation: The verb takes position 1 — the ancient flip from topic 13, still free of do. Word for word: 'Is the light out?'

nacht.context_phrase: In der Nacht ist es hier sehr ruhig.
nacht.context_translation: At night it is very quiet here.

tochter.context_phrase: Meine Tochter lernt in der Schule.
tochter.etymology_derivation: Double shift: d → t and gh → ch.

nagel.context_phrase: Er schlägt den Nagel in die Wand.
nagel.context_translation: He hammers the nail into the wall.

bär.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *berô — literally 'the brown one', a taboo-avoidance word; twin of English bear. [wiktionary]

bitter.context_phrase: Der Kaffee ohne Zucker ist bitter.
bitter.etymology_derivation: bitter — from Proto-Germanic *bitraz, the very same Germanic word as English bitter; German sources tie it to beißen (to bite), the biting taste. [wiktionary]

treppe.context_phrase: Die Kinder laufen die Treppe hoch.
treppe.context_translation: The children run up the stairs.
treppe.etymology_derivation: From West Germanic trappa, from the PIE root dreb, meaning to tread or trample; the same stepping root underlies English tread and trip. [wiktionary]

see.etymology_derivation: From Old High German sē, from Proto-West Germanic *saiwi, from Proto-Germanic *saiwiz. English sea is the listed cognate; der See is the lake, die See the sea. [wiktionary]

gefühl.context_phrase: Ich habe ein gutes Gefühl dabei.
gefühl.context_translation: I have a good feeling about it.
gefühl.etymology_derivation: ge- + fühlen (to feel — the English feel twin): a feeling is a felt thing. [wiktionary]

gemein.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *gamainī (shared, common); the page documents cognate English mean — both words slid from common to lowly to nasty. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
